abstract.p: Esophageal cancer (EC) is a frequently diagnosed malignancy with limited available treatment options. Emerging evidence has underscored the significant role of tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins in various cancers. However, the specific role of TRIM11 in EC has not been elucidated. Here, we conducted a comprehensive bioinformatics analysis, along with cell line models and animal culture experiments, to investigate the role of and molecular mechanisms through which TRIM11 contributes to EC progression, and evaluate its potential as a candidate marker associated with adverse clinicopathological features. Transcriptomic analysis was conducted using data from TCGA, GTEx, CCLE, and other publicly available databases to assess TRIM11 expression and its correlation with clinicopathological features, immune infiltration and TRIM11’s relationship with treatment response in EC. In vitro experiments showed that TRIM11 overexpression significantly promoted EC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that TRIM11 increased the proportion of cells entering the S phase. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation assays demonstrated that endogenous TRIM11 directly interacted with Axin2 and GSK3β, two core components of the β-catenin destruction complex. Additionally, TRIM11 knockdown altered the expression of key proteins in the β-catenin signaling pathway, including CyclinD1, GSK3β, Axin2, and β-catenin. Collectively, these findings highlight TRIM11 as a pro-oncogenic factor and suggest that it is a potential functional driver of EC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Esophageal cancer (EC) is a prevalent malignancy originating from the esophageal epithelium and primarily includes esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). According to global epidemiological data from 2022, EC ranks seventh among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths (4.6% of all cancer-related deaths) (Bray et al. 2024). In China, EC remains one of the deadliest malignancies, with an estimated 193,290 deaths reported in the most recent statistics (Wu et al. 2024). Survival is low in EC (20%) (Siegel et al. 2021). Strong malignancy and the absence of specific early clinical symptoms result in most patients being diagnosed at advanced stages. For locally advanced EC, neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy) is recommended to downstage the tumor and control micrometastatic disease in order to improve clinical outcomes. Despite improvements in neoadjuvant regimens, surgical techniques, and patient selection, the 5-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate following subsequent esophagectomy remains at approximately 50% (Sho Okuda 2023). Therefore, the molecular mechanisms that drive EC progression must be urgently elucidated to develop novel and effective therapeutic strategies for patients with advanced disease.

The tripartite motif (TRIM) protein family, characterized by an N-terminal TRIM region that includes a RING finger domain, predominantly functions as E3 ubiquitin ligases. These proteins regulate oncogene products and tumor suppressors through the ubiquitination and modulation of key oncogenic pathways (Hatakeyama 2011; Yamada et al. 2025). In humans, this family comprises more than 70 members (Jiaxing Wang 2025), which are critically involved in various cancers by influencing cell proliferation, DNA damage response, and apoptosis (Mohapatra et al. 2025). Among these, TRIM11, a member of the TRIM family, has been identified as an oncogenic driver in several malignancies. For instance, TRIM11 protein expression levels are significantly higher in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients than those in normal lung tissue, and significantly higher in squamous cell carcinoma than in adenocarcinoma. Patients with high TRIM11 expression have significantly worse overall 5-year survival rates (Kuempers et al. 2024). In nasopharyngeal carcinoma, TRIM11 promotes cell migration and invasion, and its expression is suppressed by the tumor suppressor p53 through direct binding to the TRIM11 promoter (Zhao et al. 2023). In prostate cancer, TRIM11 exerts oncogenic effects and is post-transcriptionally regulated by miR-5193 (Pan et al. 2023). TRIM11 also facilitates cervical cancer progression by activating the PI3K/AKT pathway (Liu et al. 2021a), and enhances chemoresistance in anaplastic thyroid cancer (Tang et al. 2021). In the digestive system, TRIM11 upregulation promotes the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) targeting the AMPK signaling pathway (Liu et al. 2021b) and gastric cancer (GC) via Axin1 regulation (Zhou et al. 2022), and can serve as a key indicator of poor prognosis. Notably, recent pan-cancer analyses have further underscored the value of multi-omics approaches in identifying novel cancer-related genes with implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and immune infiltration, including CORO1A (Elihamu et al. 2025), BYSL (Aimaiti et al. 2025), and CENPN (Jing et al. 2025), as well as disulfidptosis-related signatures (Wei et al. 2025), immune microenvironment heterogeneity (Gong et al. 2025), and metabolic features (Zhang et al. 2025) in lung adenocarcinoma. Despite its well-documented roles in various cancers, the function and clinical significance of TRIM11 in EC remain unexplored.

The tumor microenvironment (TME), composed of tumor, stromal, and infiltrating tumor-associated immune cells, plays a critical role in promoting tumor progression by inhibiting apoptosis, enabling immune evasion, and facilitating proliferation, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis in EC (Fioretzaki et al. 2025). Among stromal components, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are the most abundant. Notably, FGFR2 + CAFs secrete WNT2, which activates the Wnt/β‑catenin signaling pathway and drives malignant progression in EC (Huang et al. 2022b). Beyond these extracellular signals, the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway is also subject to regulation by intracellular factors, including TRIM-family E3 ubiquitin ligases. For instance, TRIM11 has recently been shown to promote GC progression through β‑catenin pathway activation by binding to and destabilizing Axin1, a negative regulator of this cascade (Zhou et al. 2022). As both CAF-derived WNT2 and TRIM11 converge on β‑catenin, we hypothesized that this pathway may serve as a central hub integrating stromal and intrinsic oncogenic signals in EC. Moreover, the functional relevance of Wnt/β‑catenin extends beyond tumor-cell-intrinsic effects to immune modulation. Research has shown that Wnt/β-catenin pathway disruption in GC cells inhibits their migration and invasion abilities. Notably, high β-catenin expression in GC tissues is often associated with a significant lack of CD8+ T cell infiltration, whereas low β-catenin expression combined with high PD-L1 expression confers increased sensitivity to PD-1 blockade therapy; thus, such patients may achieve a better prognosis (Li et al. 2022). Together, these findings highlight the convergence of CAF-derived signals and TRIM11 on the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Given the established links between Wnt/β-catenin signaling and immune modulation in other cancer types, this raises the possibility that TRIM11 may exert effects beyond tumor-cell-intrinsic mechanisms, a question that warrants future investigation.

In this study, we combined bioinformatic analysis with in vitro and in vivo experiments to examine the oncogenic role of TRIM11 in EC. Analysis of data from the TCGA, GEO, and GTEx databases revealed that TRIM11 is significantly overexpressed in EC and is correlated with patient diagnosis and prognosis. Functional enrichment analysis linked TRIM11 to cell cycle regulation. To further explore its immunological relevance, immune infiltration analysis was performed, which demonstrated a significant association between TRIM11 and immune cell infiltration, particularly with dendritic cells. Although TRIM11 has been established as an oncogene across various cancer types, including its role in promoting HCC through AMPK signaling and in GC via Axin1 regulation, its functional significance and mechanistic basis in EC have remained entirely unexplored. Notably, although β-catenin activation is a well-recognized oncogenic function downstream of multiple regulators, a connection between TRIM11 and the Wnt/β-catenin pathway has not been previously established in any digestive system malignancy. Thus, the specific contributions of this study are twofold: first, we identify a previously unreported mechanism by which TRIM11 stabilizes β-catenin through direct interaction with the destruction complex components Axin2 and GSK3β; second, we provide the first characterization of TRIM11’s oncogenic role in the context of EC, a malignancy in which Wnt/β-catenin signaling is particularly critical.

sec.title: Data preparing and processing
sec.p: TRIM11 mRNA expression profiles in normal human tissues were obtained from the Genotype Tissue Expression (GTEx) database (https://www.gtexportal.org/). Differences in TRIM11 expression across 33 cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were systematically analyzed and visualized using the TIMER3 web server (https://compbio.cn/timer3/), with statistical significance evaluated via differential analysis (edgeR) based on RNA-Seq raw counts. Gene expression data and clinical information for EC were downloaded from the TCGA data portal (https://tcga-data.nci.nih.gov/tcga/). After excluding patients with incomplete clinical records, 163 EC samples were analyzed. Given the limited number of EC samples in TCGA, which often restricts subgroup-specific investigations, we further validated TRIM11 expression in ESCC and EAC using the GSE26886 and GSE161533 datasets, respectively. The GSE69925 dataset, comprising 274 ESCC samples, was also included for subsequent analyses. All mRNA expression data for human EC were sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo). Data were preprocessed in R (version 4.5.2). Additionally, TRIM11 expression in tumor cell lines was examined using the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) database (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/ccle). Ethical approval and informed consent were not required for this study.

sec.title: Clinical relationship and prognostic diagnosis
sec.p: The association between TRIM11 mRNA expression and clinicopathological parameters in EC patients was evaluated using the chi-square test. To analyze the relationship between TRIM11 expression and clinical outcomes in EC patients from TCGA, Kaplan–Meier (KM) survival curves were constructed, and statistical significance was assessed using the log-rank test. These analyses were performed using the “survival” R package, and visualization was conducted via the “survminer” R package. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from diagnosis to death from any cause; relapse-free survival (RFS) as the time from initial treatment to the first recurrence; and disease-specific survival (DSS) as the time from diagnosis to death due to EC. Furthermore, the prognostic significance of TRIM11 expression in EC was examined using the “forestplot” R package.

sec.title: Co-expression network construction and functional enrichment
sec.p: To ensure the reliability of our data analysis, we first performed a systematic quality control and clustering assessment of 163 EC samples and 16 normal samples from the TCGA-EC cohort. A scale-free co‑expression network was constructed using the Weighted Gene Co‑Expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) R package, with the optimal soft-thresholding power (β) determined via the pickSoftThreshold function. A module containing TRIM11 and its constituent genes was identified and extracted. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between TRIM11‑high- and TRIM11‑low-expression groups in the GSE69925 dataset were identified using the “limma” R package, with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 as the significance threshold, yielding 3,637 DEGs. To further explore the functional roles of genes common to the TRIM11‑associated module and the DEG set, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analyses were performed using the “clusterProfiler” R package, with a false discovery rate (FDR) of < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Analysis of TRIM11 immune cell infiltration
sec.p: Within the R package “IBOR,” the CIBERSORT, ESTIMATE, MCP-counter, and TIMER algorithms were employed to assess immune cell infiltration in high- and low-TRIM11-expression groups. The results were analyzed and visualized using the “ggplot2” and “ComplexHeatmap” package in R software.

sec.title: Drug sensitivity prediction
sec.p: To evaluate the chemotherapeutic implications of TRIM11 expression, drug IC50 values were predicted using the “oncoPredict” R package based on data from the GDSC database (https://www.cancerrxgene.org/). In total, 198 drugs were assessed separately in 184 EC samples from TCGA and 274 EC samples from the GSE69925 dataset. Differences in drug sensitivity between the TRIM11-high- and TRIM11-low-expression groups were analyzed using the Wilcoxon test, with an FDR of < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: EC tissue microarray and immunohistochemistry
sec.p: The staining intensity was graded as follows: no staining (0), weakly positive (1), moderately positive (2), strongly positive (3). The percentage of positively stained cells was categorized into four grades: 0–25%, 1; 26–50%, 2; 51–75%, 3; and 76–100%, 4. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University and conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Relevant cell lines and cell culture
sec.p: All human EC cell lines (KYSE30, KYSE450, and Eca109) and the human normal esophageal epithelial cell line, Het-1 A, were obtained from the China Center for Type Culture Collection. All cell lines used in this study (KYSE30, KYSE450, Eca109, and Het-1 A) were authenticated using short tandem repeat (STR) profiling prior to the experiments. The STR profiles were compared with the official databases (e.g., ATCC, DSMZ, or Cellosaurus), and all cell lines showed ≥ 80% matching with their reference profiles, confirming their identities (Fig. S3). The cells were cultured in DMEM/F12 medium (Hyclone, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, USA). All cell lines were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2.

sec.title: Virus transfection for lentivirus
sec.p: The pLVX-Puro lentiviral vector contained the full-length coding sequence (CDS) of TRIM11. HEK 293T cells were transfected with the pLV-Puro-TRIM11 expression plasmid and packaging plasmids using Lipofectamine™ 2000 (Invitrogen, USA). Lentiviral supernatants were collected. Additionally, four types of lentiviral supernatants—expressing either control short-hairpin RNA (designated as shRNA) or TRIM11-specific shRNAs (designated as shTRIM11-1, shTRIM11-2, and shTRIM11-3)—were purchased from Shanghai GeneChem Co., Ltd. (China). The following shRNA sequences were used: shTRIM11-1 (GCTTGCTAAGATGGCCGAGAT), shTRIM11-2 (GGAGAAGTCACTGGAGCATCT), shTRIM11-3 (GCTGATCCTGTCTGAAGACAG), and shNC (TTCTCCGAACGTGTCACGT). All supernatants described above were added to the EC cell lines to facilitate transfection.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, China) was used to isolate proteins from the cultured cells. Protein concentrations were quantified using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay kit (Beyotime, China). After separation using 10% SDS-PAGE, the proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (Millipore, USA) for 1.5 h. The membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat dry milk in Tris-buffered saline containing Tween 20 (TBST) at room temperature for 1 h. After blocking, membranes were incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. After washing three times with TBST, the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies at 37 °C for 60 min. Protein expression levels were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection system (Bio-Rad, USA). Target protein expression was normalized to that of GAPDH in the same lane. Densitometric analyses were performed using three independent biological replicates (n = 3), with representative blots shown in the main figures.

sec.title: Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays
sec.p: To verify endogenous protein interactions, Co-IP assays were performed using Eca109 cells. Cells were treated with 20 µM of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h prior to lysis to stabilize potential protein complexes. Subsequently, cells were lysed in ice-cold immunoprecipitation (IP) lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. An aliquot of the lysate was used as an input. Equal amounts of cell lysates were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following antibodies: anti-TRIM11 (Proteintech), anti-Axin2 (Cell Signaling Technology), anti-GSK3β (Proteintech), or control normal IgG (see Table S2 for antibody details). Protein A/G agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were then added and incubated for 4 h. The immunocomplexes were washed extensively, separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and analyzed by immunoblotting using the indicated antibodies.

sec.title: CCK8 cell viability assay
sec.p: Cell proliferation was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (Beyotime, China). EC cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 2,000 cells per well. After incubation at 37 °C for 0, 24, 48, or 72 h, optical density (OD) at 450 nm was measured to assess cell viability.

sec.title: Colony formation assay
sec.p: EC cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 5,000 cells per well. After 14 days of incubation, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 15 min.

sec.title: Cell-cycle analysis
sec.p: EC cells were seeded into 6-well plates and cultured until they reached 60–70% confluence, followed by 24 h of serum starvation. After removing the old medium, the cells were replenished with DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% FBS and incubated for a further 24 h. Subsequently, the cells were fixed with 75% cold ethanol at − 20 °C overnight. For cell cycle analysis, each sample was treated with propidium iodide (PI) and RNase, and incubated at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. Finally, the cell cycle distribution was assessed using flow cytometry (Beckman Coulter, USA), and the data were analyzed using FlowJoV10 software.

sec.title: Transwell migration and invasion assay
sec.p: Transwell migration and invasion assays were conducted using Transwell plates equipped with 8-µm pore filters (Costar, USA). For each well, 5 × 10⁴ EC cells were seeded into the upper chamber in 0.2 mL of serum-free medium, whereas 0.6 mL of medium containing 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber. For the invasion assay, the chambers were pre-coated with Matrigel (BD Biosciences, USA), whereas the migration assay was performed without coating. After incubation at 37 °C for 48 (migration assay) or 72 h (invasion assay), non-migrated or non-invaded cells on the upper surface of the membrane were carefully removed using a cotton swab. Cells that migrated to or invaded the lower surface of the membrane were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with 0.5% crystal violet. All experiments were performed in triplicate.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: Cells were seeded in a 24-well plate at a density of 1 × 10⁴ cells per well and cultured for 24 h to allow attachment to coverslips. After fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde, the cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 and blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Beijing Solarbio Science and Technology Co., Ltd., China). The cells on the coverslips were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody against β-catenin (1:100 dilution, Proteintech, China). The following day, the cells were incubated with Cy3-labeled fluorescent secondary antibodies (1:100 dilution; Proteintech, China) for 1 h. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Beyotime, China). Finally, the stained cells were visualized using a laser scanning confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan, model FV1200). ImageJ software was used for quantification. At least 50 cells were analyzed in each group. The nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio was calculated as the mean fluorescence intensity in the nuclear region divided by that in the cytoplasmic region, and the nuclei were identified using DAPI staining. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM with individual data points.

sec.title: Tumor xenograft model
sec.p: The animal studies included in this project were approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (approval number: IACUC-20201212). Five-week-old male BALB/c nude mice were obtained from Beijing Life River Experimental Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (China). KYSE30-NC, KKYSE30-OE, KYSE450-NC, and KYSE450-Sh, along with Eca109-NC and Eca109Sh cells, were washed in serum-free RPMI 1640 and subcutaneously injected into the right flank of the dorsal region of nude mice, with six mice in each group. Each mouse was injected subcutaneously with 1 × 106/mL cells. Tumor growth was monitored every four days after an initial observation period of 2 weeks, and tumor volume was measured using the following formula: volume = length × width2 × 0.5. After allowing tumors to form for 30 days, the mice were euthanized and tissues were collected for volume and weight measurements.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (La Jolla, USA). All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates (n = 3 per group), and data are presented as the mean ± SEM. For two-group comparisons, the equality of variances was assessed using the F-test. Student’s t-test was used for comparisons with equal variances (F-test, P > 0.05), while Welch’s t-test was applied for unequal variances (F-test, P < 0.05). For comparisons among three or more groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or Welch’s ANOVA was used based on variance homogeneity, followed by Bonferroni post hoc correction; when normality was violated, the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test was applied. For clinical and survival analyses, Fisher’s exact test was used for clinicopathological correlations, survival curves were analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method with the log-rank test, and Cox regression was used for multivariate analysis. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. 3.

sec.title: TRIM11 was highly expressed in EC
sec.p: The basal expression level of TRIM11 in normal human tissues was assessed using RNA-Seq data from the GTEx database. TRIM11 was highly expressed in most of the normal tissues, including the esophagus (Fig. 1A). Consistent with this finding, analysis of the CCLE database indicated elevated TRIM11 expression in multiple tumor cell lines (Fig. 1B). We further evaluated TRIM11 mRNA expression across 33 cancer types using TCGA data, which revealed significant upregulation in 17 malignancies, including EC, compared with matched normal tissues, whereas kidney chromophobe (KICH) exhibited notable downregulation (Fig. 1C). Given the limited number of normal esophageal samples in TCGA, we integrated normal esophageal epithelial RNA expression data from both TCGA and GTEx databases to further investigate the role of TRIM11 in EC. After a comprehensive batch-effect correction using ComBat (Fig. S1; Table S1), TRIM11 was significantly overexpressed in EC tissues compared with normal controls (Fig. 1D). Consistent with this, analysis of the TCGA cohort and GSE26886 dataset demonstrated that TRIM11 expression was markedly increased in both ESCC and EAC, with no significant difference between the two histological subtypes (Figs. 1E–F). Subsequent validation using the GSE161533 dataset further corroborated elevated TRIM11 expression in EC, reinforcing our initial observations (Fig. 1G).

sec.title: Elevated TRIM11 expression is associated with poor prognosis in EC patients
sec.p: As summarized in Table 1, high TRIM11 expression was significantly correlated with lymph node metastasis (P = 0.010), with 63.4% (52/82) of patients in the high-expression group presenting with nodal involvement (N1–N3) compared with 42.0% (34/81) in the low-expression group. No significant associations were observed between sex, age, T stage, and distant metastasis (all P > 0.05). Kaplan–Meier analysis based on TCGA data was performed to evaluate the association between TRIM11 expression and patient survival. OS, RFS, and DSS were defined as described in the Methods. Patients with high TRIM11 expression showed a significantly shorter OS (Fig. 2A), whereas no significant differences were observed in RFS or DSS (Figs. 2B–C). Univariate Cox regression identified high TRIM11 expression (HR = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.01–2.73, P = 0.045), advanced N stage, and advanced pathological stage as significant risk factors for poorer OS. However, in multivariate analysis adjusting for age, T stage, N stage, and pathological stage, only advanced pathological stage remained an independent prognostic predictor (HR = 2.18, 95% CI: 1.12–4.27, P = 0.022), whereas the association with TRIM11 expression was attenuated (HR = 1.43, 95% CI: 0.84–2.44, P = 0.187) (Figs. 2D–E). To further validate these findings, immunohistochemical staining was performed using a tissue microarray containing 34 paired EC and adjacent normal samples. High TRIM11 expression (staining index > 4, Fig. 2F) was significantly correlated with an advanced clinical stage (P < 0.0001, Table S3). Together, these results suggest a potential association between elevated TRIM11 expression and adverse clinicopathological features in EC, although validation in larger cohorts is warranted. This suggests that, although TRIM11 expression is significantly associated with lymph node metastasis and poorer OS in univariate analysis, its prognostic value may largely depend on or be confounded by conventional clinicopathological factors such as pathological stage.

sec.title: Coexpression network construction and functional enrichment
sec.p: Data quality control was implemented using the hclust function. After applying a cut-off height, one outlier sample was removed (Fig. 3A). WGCNA was performed using the R package “WGCNA” by applying average linkage hierarchical clustering (Fig. 3B), resulting in the identification of 11 distinct co‑expression modules, each represented by a unique color (Fig. 3C). As shown in Fig. 3D, the target gene TRIM11 was assigned to the blue module, which displayed a strong positive correlation with sample type (r = 0.601, P = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸), indicating that genes within this were are markedly upregulated in tumor tissues. Furthermore, the blue module exhibited a significant negative correlation with age (r = − 0.287, P = 0.00013) and a positive correlation with T stage (r = 0.171, P = 0.025), suggesting its potential involvement in tumor initiation and progression. Thus, the blue module containing TRIM11 appears to be highly active in tumor tissues and may represent a tumor-associated functional unit worthy of further experimental validation. To further explore the functional relevance of TRIM11, we intersected 3,489 genes from the blue module with the 1,176 DEGs identified in the GSE69925 dataset to obtain 624 overlapping genes (Fig. 3E). Functional enrichment analyses, including GO and KEGG pathway analyses, were performed on the overlapping gene sets. The top 10 enriched GO terms and top 20 enriched KEGG pathways are presented. In the biological process category, “chromosome segregation” was the most significantly enriched term, whereas “chromosomal region” ranked highest in the cellular component category, and “ATP hydrolysis activity” was the most prominent term in the molecular function category (Fig. 3F). Additionally, KEGG analysis revealed “cell cycle” as the most significantly enriched pathway (Fig. 3G).

sec.title: Immune infiltrating analysis
sec.p: To evaluate differences in immune cell infiltration between high- and low-TRIM11‑expressing subgroups in EC, we applied multiple deconvolution algorithms, including CIBERSORT, ESTIMATE, MCP‑counter, and TIMER, to the TCGA‑EC dataset. A summary of the immune cell proportions in patients with EC is presented in Fig. 4A. Consistent with the analytical methods, tumors with high TRIM11 expression showed markedly lower stromal, immune, and ESTIMATE combined scores and elevated tumor purity (Fig. 4B). These findings indicate a depleted immune and stromal landscape in high-TRIM11 tumors, supporting a link between TRIM11 and the immunosuppressive TME. Thus, TRIM11 may be a candidate biomarker for identifying patients who are less likely to benefit from an immune checkpoint blockade. Further characterization using the MCP‑counter and TIMER algorithms identified dendritic cells (DCs) as the immune subset most strongly and negatively correlated with TRIM11 expression (Figs. 4C–D). Additionally, TIMER analysis revealed inverse associations of TRIM11 with CD8⁺ T cells and macrophages, whereas MCP‑counter indicated a negative correlation with fibroblasts. Computational analysis using the ESTIMATE algorithm revealed a correlation between higher TRIM11 expression and lower immune/stromal scores, as well as higher tumor purity scores in TCGA-EC samples. However, these findings were derived from transcriptomic data and require histological validation.

sec.title: TRIM11 overexpression induced proliferation, cell migration, and invasion in EC
sec.p: We evaluated the expression levels of TRIM11 in human EC cell lines (KYSE30, Eca109, and KYSE450) and in the normal human esophageal epithelial cell line Het-1A. As shown in Fig. 5A, TRIM11 protein expression was significantly higher in the Eca109 (P < 0.01) and KYSE450 (P < 0.05) cells than that in Het-1A cells. In contrast, TRIM11 expression in KYSE30 was slightly lower than that in Het-1A cells (P < 0.05).

To investigate the biological role of TRIM11 in EC, we established TRIM11 knockdown and overexpression cell lines using lentivirus transfection. Three cell lines were selected for this purpose: Eca109 and KYSE450 for TRIM11 knockdown, and KYSE30 for TRIM11 overexpression. Control short hairpin RNA (NC) did not affect TRIM11 mRNA expression compared with wild-type (WT) cells. Western blot analysis confirmed that TRIM11 protein levels were effectively suppressed or elevated following lentivirus transfection (Fig. 5B).

Based on the western blotting results, the lentivirus containing shTRIM11-3 demonstrated excellent knockdown efficiency. Therefore, we selected Eca109 and KYSE450 cells transfected with lentivirus (hereafter referred to as Eca109Sh and KYSE450Sh, respectively) for subsequent in vitro experiments. To evaluate the effect of TRIM11 on EC cell proliferation, KYSE30 cells overexpressing TRIM11 exhibited an increased colony-forming ability, whereas TRIM11 knockdown inhibited colony growth (Fig. 5C). To further validate the role of TRIM11 in EC growth in vivo, EC cells with stable TRIM11 knockdown or overexpression were subcutaneously injected into the right dorsal flank of nude mice. After 30 days, the tumor volume was measured. The gross morphological appearance of tumor-bearing nude mice provides a visual representation of tumor size. Our results clearly indicated that genetic knockdown of TRIM11 significantly reduced tumor volume and weight, whereas overexpression of TRIM11 exhibited the opposite trend (Fig. 5D). Additionally, we performed CCK-8 assays. As shown in Figs. 6A-C, the proliferation of Eca109 and KYSE450 cells was significantly suppressed 24, 48, and 72 h after TRIM11 knockdown via lentivirus transfection. In contrast, TRIM11 overexpression enhanced KYSE30 cell proliferation. Furthermore, cell migration and invasion were markedly enhanced in KYSE30 cells overexpressing TRIM11 (Fig. 6D) but were significantly reduced in Eca109 and KYSE450 cells following TRIM11 knockdown (Figs. 6E–F). These findings suggested that TRIM11 promotes the oncogenic properties of EC.

sec.title: TRIM11 increased the proportion of cells in S phase in EC cell lines
sec.p: To investigate the role of TRIM11 in cell cycle regulation, we performed propidium iodide (PI) staining and flow cytometry. TRIM11 overexpression significantly decreased the percentage of cells in the G1 phase and increased the proportion of cells in the G2 and S phases (Fig. 7A and D). Conversely, TRIM11 knockdown in Eca109 cells led to a notable increase in the G1-phase population and a decrease in the S-phase population (Fig. 7B and E). In KYSE450 cells, TRIM11 knockdown specifically inhibited the S phase without significantly affecting other phases (Fig.7C and F). These results indicated that TRIM11 played a critical role in modulating cell cycle progression in EC cells.

sec.title: TRIM11 regulated β-catenin signaling pathway
sec.p: Accumulating evidence suggests that the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway plays a critical role in the development and progression of EC. Our western blot analysis revealed that knockdown of TRIM11 in Eca109 and KYSE450 cells significantly downregulated the expression of Cyclin D1 and β-catenin while upregulating GSK3β and Axin2. Conversely, TRIM11 overexpression in KYSE30 cells produced the opposite effect (Figs. 8A–C). Immunofluorescence analysis was performed to assess the subcellular localization of β-catenin. TRIM11 overexpression promoted the translocation of β-catenin translocation from the cytoplasm to the nucleus (Figs. 8D–F). These findings suggest that TRIM11 exerts oncogenic effects by modulating the β-catenin signaling pathway.

sec.title: TRIM11 endogenously interacts with core components of the β-catenin destruction complex
sec.p: Given the regulatory effect of TRIM11 on the β-catenin signaling pathway, we sought to further investigate its underlying molecular mechanism, specifically its potential physical association with key regulatory complexes. Although the aforementioned experiments (Fig. 8A-F) indicated that TRIM11 could modulate β-catenin stability, whether it directly associates with destruction complex components remains unclear. To verify this direct physical interaction, we performed Co-IP assays in Eca109 cells endogenously expressing TRIM11. Cells were treated with MG132 prior to lysis to stabilize transient interactions and prevent proteasome-mediated degradation. As shown in Fig. 9, immunoprecipitation of endogenous TRIM11 using a specific antibody resulted in successful endogenous Axin2 and GSK3β co-precipitation. Conversely, reciprocal Co-IP using antibodies against Axin2 specifically pulled down endogenous TRIM11. These interactions were not detected in control samples using non-specific IgG, confirming their specificity. Our results provide direct evidence that TRIM11 forms an endogenous protein complex with Axin2 and GSK3β in EC cells, offering mechanistic support for its role in modulating the β-catenin pathway by physically targeting the destruction complex.

sec.title: TRIM11 expression is associated with sensitivity and resistance to anticancer drugs
sec.p: Drug response prediction was performed on 184 EC samples from TCGA (Figs. 10A–Q) and 274 EC samples from the GSE69925 dataset (Figs S4A–Q). A total of 17 drug-sensitivity predictions related to TRIM11 expression were identified based on the TCGA and GSE69925 datasets. High TRIM11 expression correlated with increased IC50 values for 16 anticancer agents, including SB216763, KU-55,933, NU7441, Doramapimod, RO-3306, AZD8055, and PRIMA-1MET, suggesting decreased drug sensitivity, whereas it was associated with lower IC50 values for lapatinib. It should be noted that these findings were derived from computational predictions without multiple comparison correction; therefore, they should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating observations that require experimental validation.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: EC is a prevalent malignancy that often lacks specific clinical symptoms in its early stages, leading to most diagnoses occurring in patients with advanced, metastatic disease. Although neoadjuvant therapy or radical radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy represent the current standard of care for locally advanced EC, the clinical outcomes remain unsatisfactory, with recurrence rates reaching 30–50% (Wang et al. 2022). Traditional therapeutic approaches are ineffective for patients with EC. Therefore, it is essential to identify novel therapeutic biomarkers and signaling axes in EC. Such discoveries will allow the mechanisms of chemoresistance to be elucidated, with the ultimate goal of enhancing patient responsiveness to chemotherapy and improving clinical outcomes. A recent study has shown that E2F1 reduces the sensitivity of EC cells to sorafenib via the miR-29c-3p/COL11A1 axis, suggesting that targeting the E2F1-mediated pathway in combination with sorafenib represents a promising therapeutic strategy for EC (Ma et al. 2023). Transcription factor YY2 is critically involved in the pathogenesis of EC. Currently, there are no therapeutic agents that specifically target YY2 gene. As such, YY2 holds promise as a prognostic biomarker and novel therapeutic target for EC patients (Gou et al. 2025). Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying EC is crucial for the development of novel therapeutic strategies and identification of potential therapeutic targets.

In this study, we identified TRIM11 as a pro-oncogenic factor in EC. Although multivariate analysis indicated that its prognostic significance was not independent of the pathological stage, elevated TRIM11 expression was significantly correlated with aggressive clinicopathological features, such as lymph node metastasis and poor OS in univariate analysis. Although the strong association between high TRIM11 expression and advanced clinical stage was statistically significant (P < 0.0001), these findings should be considered preliminary and warrant validation in larger independent cohorts. Additionally, bioinformatics analysis revealed a negative correlation between TRIM11 expression and dendritic cell infiltration, suggesting a potential link to immune modulation. These immune infiltration analyses are algorithm‑based and lack histological validation. Therefore, they should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require experimental confirmation via immunohistochemistry in future studies. Drug‑sensitivity predictions based on the TCGA‑EC and GSE69925 datasets indicated that TRIM11 expression may predict responses to certain therapeutic agents, including immunotherapy. In vitro functional assays revealed that TRIM11 knockout significantly suppressed the proliferation, migration, and invasion of EC cells, accompanied by downregulation of Cyclin D1 and β‑catenin expression. In vivo xenograft models confirmed that TRIM11 depletion markedly inhibited tumor growth. Our study found that TRIM11 knockdown led to the downregulation of β-catenin and its downstream target genes. Mechanistically, we discovered that TRIM11 physically interacts with Axin2 and GSK3β, which are core components of the β-catenin destruction complex. This finding is crucial as it directly explains how TRIM11 may influence the stability of β-catenin. The endogenous interaction confirmed by Co-IP assays suggested that TRIM11 may function as a novel regulator of this complex. One possible mechanism is that TRIM11, which functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, disrupts the stability or function of the entire destruction complex by mediating the ubiquitination and degradation of Axin2 or GSK3β, thereby indirectly leading to β-catenin accumulation. Alternatively, TRIM11 may act as a scaffold protein within the complex, influencing its assembly or activity. Although further investigation is required to determine whether TRIM11 directly ubiquitinates these substrates, the physical interaction evidence presented here strongly supports a direct and critical role for TRIM11 in β-catenin pathway regulation, echoing the functions reported for other TRIM family proteins in Wnt signaling. Although univariate analysis suggested a significant association between high TRIM11 expression and poorer OS, this association was attenuated after adjusting for pathological stage and nodal status in multivariate Cox regression. This suggests that the prognostic impact of TRIM11 is largely mediated by its close relationship with established prognostic factors, particularly lymph node metastasis. Therefore, rather than serving as an independent prognostic biomarker, TRIM11 may function as a molecular correlate of aggressive tumor behavior, and its measurement could complement conventional staging systems to refine risk stratification in patients with EC. Taken together, these findings highlight TRIM11 as a candidate marker for adverse clinicopathological features.

The tripartite motif (TRIM) protein family encompasses a group of ubiquitously expressed proteins that play pivotal roles in diverse cellular processes, including cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and signal transduction (Huang et al. 2022a). TRIM11 has emerged as a recognized oncogene in multiple cancer types, including HCC, GC, lung cancer, and breast cancer. Mechanistically, TRIM11 promotes tumor progression through diverse pathways. Despite these established oncogenic roles, the function of TRIM11 in EC remains largely unexplored, and whether it exerts its effects through similar signaling axes—particularly the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway—has yet to be determined. This study therefore aimed to investigate the role of TRIM11 in EC progression and its potential mechanistic link to Wnt/β‑catenin signaling. Aberrant activation of the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway, often due to genetic mutations, is implicated in the pathogenesis of various human cancers. Notably, several TRIM family proteins function as oncogenes by activating the TRIM pathway. For instance, in gliomas, TRIM29 drives tumor growth and invasion by regulating the Wnt/Dvl2/β‑catenin axis (Cao et al. 2019). Similarly, TRIM59 is upregulated in neuroblastoma and promotes proliferation via the Wnt/β-catenin pathway (Chen et al. 2019). In HCC, TRIM66 acts as an oncogene by facilitating Wnt/β‑catenin signaling (Fan et al. 2019). Furthermore, TRIM11 promotes GC progression by binding to Axin1, destabilizing this negative regulator and consequently activating the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway (Zhou et al. 2022).

In this study, we demonstrated that TRIM11 knockdown significantly arrested cell cycle progression in the G1 phase and decreased the population of cells in the S/G2 phase, whereas TRIM11 overexpression produced the opposite effects. Previous studies have established that lung cancer cell proliferation is associated with Wnt/β-catenin pathway activation (Xiong et al. 2020); therefore, we examined this pathway in our models. Both TRIM11 and β‑catenin protein levels were markedly elevated in TRIM11‑overexpressing KYSE30 cells. Conversely, TRIM11 downregulation strongly suppressed the proliferation of Eca109 and KYSE450 cells, inducing G1 phase arrest accompanied by reduced expression of β‑catenin and cyclin D1. Cyclin D1, the overexpression of which is known to drive cell cycle progression by facilitating the G1‑S transition (Lukas et al. 1995), was similarly modulated in our experiments. β-catenin, a key downstream effector of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, plays a critical role in epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Komiya and Habas 2008). Consistent with this, Transwell assays revealed that TRIM11 overexpression enhanced the migration and invasion capabilities of EC cells, which was consistent with our western blot findings. Additionally, GSK3β, a known tumor suppressor in the β-catenin/Wnt signaling pathway (Pecoraro et al. 2021), exhibited decreased protein levels in TRIM11-overexpressing Kyse30 cells, whereas its levels were upregulated following TRIM11 knockdown. Our findings align with previous reports implicating TRIM family members in Wnt/β‑catenin regulation across various cancer types, while uniquely identifying TRIM11 as a modulator of this pathway in EC. Notably, our data suggest that TRIM11 may act upstream of β‑catenin, potentially through its E3 ligase activity, though the precise molecular mechanism warrants further investigation.

DCs, as professional antigen-presenting cells, play a crucial role in antitumor immunity. Following the capture of tumor antigens, DCs migrate to the draining lymph nodes, where they present molecular markers and metabolites from tumor cells to activate and proliferate T lymphocytes (Matsuo et al. 2021; Sharma et al. 2024). Notably, reduced DC infiltration within tumors has been associated with poor clinical outcomes in multiple solid malignancies (Plumas 2021). Therefore, a deeper understanding of the TME is essential for rational drug design and improved patient prognosis. For example, combining PD-L1 blockade with a DC vaccine has been shown to promote significant tumor regression by depleting PD-L1⁺ macrophages, suppressing bone marrow inflammation, and enhancing stem-cell-like memory T cell responses (Sprooten et al. 2024). Similarly, low levels of tumor-infiltrating DCs have been linked to adverse prognostic factors in EC, including lymph node metastasis, advanced TNM stage, and larger lesion sizes (Pei et al. 2021). In this study, TRIM11 expression showed a significant negative correlation with DC infiltration, suggesting that TRIM11 contributes to the modulation of the TME in EC. These findings highlight a potential mechanism through which TRIM11 facilitates immune evasion and promotes tumor progression in this malignancy. Beyond its cell-intrinsic role in promoting proliferation, the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is also a well-established TME modulator (Huang et al. 2024; Mortezaee 2024). Specifically, a key mechanism by which tumor-intrinsic β-catenin signaling promotes immune evasion involves transcriptional silencing of the chemokine CCL4, resulting in defective recruitment of Batf3-lineage DCs and a subsequent lack of T-cell infiltration (Spranger et al. 2015). This paradigm establishes a direct link between aberrant β-catenin activation and immune exclusion. As TRIM11 stabilizes β-catenin and activates its transcriptional output (Fig. 8), it is plausible that TRIM11 may also contribute to the establishment of an immune-cold phenotype in EC. Elevated TRIM11 expression could repress DC-attracting chemokine expression via the β-catenin axis, thereby hindering anti-tumor immunity. This hypothesis is consistent with the emerging role of TRIM-family proteins in immune regulation. Collectively, emerging evidence on ESCC and other squamous cell carcinomas highlights diverse mechanisms by which tumor-intrinsic factors, including metabolic transporters (Zheng et al. 2023), immune-regulatory protein interactions (Luo et al. 2025), and oncogenic mutations (He et al. 2024), shape immune cell infiltration and therapeutic responses. These findings support the relevance of our observation that TRIM11 may contribute to immune exclusion in EC, warranting further mechanistic investigations. We acknowledge that the observed correlation between TRIM11 expression and DC infiltration was derived from bioinformatic analysis and did not establish a causal relationship. Functional studies, such as immune cell co-culture systems or in vivo models with immune-competent mice, are required to determine whether TRIM11-mediated β-catenin activation directly contributes to immune evasion in EC.

We employed the GDSC database to predict the chemotherapy response based on TRIM11 expression, revealing correlations between TRIM11 expression levels and IC50 values for 17 anticancer agents. However, given the exploratory nature of this analysis and the lack of multiple comparison correction, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating, rather than definitive. Similarly, this study did not directly address the potential role of TRIM11 in immune modulation, as we did not assess PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, or conduct functional assays involving immune cells. Although Wnt/β‑catenin signaling has been associated with immune evasion in other contexts, any speculation regarding TRIM11 as a predictor of the immunotherapy response remains hypothetical. Collectively, these limitations underscore the fact that the proposed links among TRIM11, drug sensitivity, and immune modulation are exploratory. Future studies incorporating functional drug sensitivity assays, immune cell coculture systems, and validation in independent patient cohorts, including in vivo studies with immunocompetent hosts, are necessary to determine whether TRIM11 expression is useful for informing treatment decisions.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, regarding the functional experiments, while we observed consistent effects of TRIM11 modulation across multiple cell lines, the experimental design was asymmetric, with one overexpression line (KYSE30) and two knockdown lines (Eca109 and KYSE450). This was due to the differential endogenous expression of TRIM11 across the available EC cell lines and the optimization of transfection efficiency. Future studies employing additional overexpression and knockdown models with a more balanced design would strengthen these conclusions further. Second, although our study established a direct physical interaction between TRIM11 and the β-catenin destruction complex components Axin2 and GSK3β (Fig. 9), several mechanistic questions remain unanswered. Rescue experiments, such as β-catenin knockdown or expression of a constitutively active β-catenin mutant, are necessary to definitively establish the causal relationship between TRIM11 and β-catenin in mediating the observed phenotypes. Additionally, whether TRIM11 promotes β-catenin stabilization by inhibiting its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation warrants future investigation using ubiquitination assays. The potential metabolic functions downstream of TRIM11‑mediated β‑catenin activation, including glycolytic reprogramming, also remain to be explored. Third, the bioinformatic analyses presented in this study, including chemotherapy response predictions and immune infiltration correlations, were exploratory in nature. The drug sensitivity findings derived from the GDSC database lacked multiple comparison correction and experimental validation, and the immune-related analyses did not incorporate direct measurements, such as PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, or functional immune cell assays. Although Wnt/β‑catenin signaling has been associated with immune evasion in other contexts, any speculation regarding TRIM11 as a predictor of the immunotherapy response remains hypothetical. Future studies incorporating functional drug sensitivity assays, immune cell co-culture systems, and validation in independent patient cohorts, including in vivo studies with immunocompetent hosts, are necessary to determine whether TRIM11 expression is useful for informing treatment decisions. Despite these limitations, the direct binding data presented here provide a solid foundation for understanding how TRIM11 engages the destruction complex to modulate β-catenin signaling in EC.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: TRIM11 is frequently overexpressed in EC, where it correlates with lymph node metastasis and promotes malignant phenotypes via the β-catenin pathway. Its negative association with dendritic cell infiltration suggests a potential link with immune modulation; however, this requires further experimental validation. Together, these findings suggest that TRIM11 is a pro-oncogenic factor in EC and suggest its potential as a candidate therapeutic target for further investigation.
